skills.name: Find percentage errors and the greatest and least values from approximations

note.text:
Percentage error = relative error × 100% = (absolute error ÷ true value) × 100%.
A value rounded to a unit has a lower bound (half a unit below) and an upper bound (half a unit above): 7 cm to the nearest cm is between 6.5 cm and 7.5 cm.
Greatest and least values of a calculation:
• sum: greatest = upper + upper; least = lower + lower.
• difference a − b: greatest = upper a − lower b; least = lower a − upper b.
• product (positive numbers): greatest = upper × upper; least = lower × lower.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to work out percentage errors and the greatest and least values of sums, differences and products of rounded measurements.
Builds on: Lesson {33} (absolute and relative error) and Lesson {32} (bounds).
Leads to: accuracy in Physics practicals and upper and lower bounds in Form Five.

sections.heading: Percentage error
sections.text:
Percentage error = (absolute error ÷ true value) × {100}%.
A bottle holding {500} ml measured as {490} ml: absolute error {10} ml, relative error {10} ÷ {500} = {0.02}, percentage error {2}%.
Always divide by the true value.

sections.heading: Greatest and least values
sections.text:
{12} cm to the nearest cm lies between {11.5} cm and {12.5} cm. Use these bounds to find the extreme answers.
• Sum {12} + {8}: greatest {12.5} + {8.5} = {21}; least {11.5} + {7.5} = {19}.
• Difference {12} − {8}: greatest {12.5} − {7.5} = {5}; least {11.5} − {8.5} = {3}.
• Area {12} × {8}: greatest {12.5} × {8.5} = {106.25}; least {11.5} × {7.5} = {86.25}.
For a difference, the greatest uses the larger value's upper bound and the smaller value's lower bound.

key_words.meaning: the largest value that rounds to the given value
the smallest value that rounds to the given value

examples: {20} m to the nearest m: bounds {19.5} m and {20.5} m

mistake.why: To make a difference as large as possible, take as much as possible away from as little as possible.

worked_example.problem: A rectangle measures {l} cm by {w} cm, each to the nearest cm. Find the greatest possible perimeter.

cards.idea: To the nearest unit, the bounds are half a unit below and above.
example: {7} cm to the nearest cm: from {6.5} cm to {7.5} cm

cards.idea: Greatest sum: add the upper bounds. Greatest difference: upper minus lower.
example: {12} cm and {8} cm (nearest cm): greatest sum {21} cm; greatest difference {12.5} − {7.5} = {5} cm

check.prompt: Two lengths are {a} cm and {b} cm, each to the nearest cm. What is the greatest possible total length?

misconceptions.explain: Each length could be up to {0.5} cm more: add the upper bounds.
Both lengths can be {0.5} cm more: add {0.5} twice.

questions.prompt: The true volume of a bottle is {t} ml. It is measured as {m} ml. What is the percentage error?

misconceptions.explain: Multiply the relative error by {100} to get a percentage.
Divide by the true value {t}, not the measured value.

questions.prompt: A mass is {x} kg to the nearest {u} kg. What is its lower bound, in kg?

misconceptions.explain: Go down half a unit, not a whole unit.

questions.prompt: Two lengths are {a} cm and {b} cm, each to the nearest cm. What is the greatest possible total length?

misconceptions.explain: Each length could be up to {0.5} cm more: add the upper bounds.
Both lengths can be {0.5} cm more: add {0.5} twice.

questions.prompt: A rectangular plot is {l} m by {w} m, each to the nearest metre. What is the least possible area, in m²?

misconceptions.explain: Each side could be up to {0.5} m less: use the lower bounds.
Use the lower bound of each side, then multiply.

questions.prompt: A plank {a} cm long (to the nearest cm) has {b} cm (to the nearest cm) cut off. What is the greatest possible length left?

misconceptions.explain: Using upper − upper keeps the same difference. For the greatest, subtract the least cut.
That is the least length left (lower − upper).

solution: Greatest left = greatest start − least cut.
